The word paddy has two completely separate meanings that have nothing to do with each other. Context always makes it clear which one is being used.

This is by far the most common and widely used meaning of the word.

What it means

Paddy refers to rice — but specifically rice in its natural, raw, unprocessed state, still wrapped in its outer shell (called a husk). When rice is harvested from the plant, it doesn't look like the clean white grains you cook at home. It still has a tough, brownish-golden covering around each grain. That grain, with the husk still on, is called paddy (or sometimes paddy rice or rough rice).

Once farmers remove the husk, it becomes brown rice. After further processing to strip away more layers, it becomes the familiar white rice people eat. So "paddy" is essentially rice at its most natural stage — straight from the plant, before any processing.

Paddy fields

By natural extension, paddy also refers to the fields where rice is grown. A paddy field (sometimes called a paddy on its own) is a flooded, muddy field in which rice plants grow. Rice needs standing water around its roots for much of its growing period, so these fields are deliberately kept wet or completely submerged in water during the growing season.

Paddy fields are a defining feature of agriculture across South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, and parts of Africa. The terraced, water-filled rice fields you might have seen in pictures from places like Bali, Vietnam, or the Indian countryside — those are paddy fields.

Examples in use:

  • "The farmers harvested thousands of tonnes of paddy this season."
  • "The village was surrounded by green paddy fields as far as the eye could see."
  • "Paddy cultivation requires careful management of water levels throughout the season."

Important distinction

When someone says "paddy" in an agricultural or food context, they almost always mean rice — either the grain in its husk, or the field where it's grown. The two usages are closely connected: paddy (the crop) grows in paddy (the field).
Meaning 2: A fit of anger or temper (informal, British and Irish)

This meaning is entirely unrelated to rice. It is informal and mainly used in British and Irish English.

What it means

A paddy (in this sense) is a sudden burst of bad temper — a childish or irrational fit of anger, frustration, or sulking. It's the kind of rage or tantrum where someone overreacts, storms off, or makes a fuss over something that perhaps doesn't deserve such a strong reaction.

It's often used with the phrases "in a paddy" (meaning currently angry) or "throw a paddy" (meaning to have or perform this tantrum).

Examples in use:

  • "He threw a complete paddy when the restaurant got his order wrong."
  • "Don't get in a paddy over such a small thing."
  • "She stormed off in a paddy after losing the argument."

Register and tone

This is a casual, informal word. You wouldn't use it in a formal letter or serious writing. It's the kind of word someone uses when telling a story about someone overreacting: slightly amused, slightly dismissive of the anger. It often carries a tone suggesting the anger was unnecessary or excessive.
Quick summary of the two meanings

Paddy (meaning 1) — Rice in its unprocessed, husked state; or the flooded field where rice is grown. Used globally, especially in agriculture, food, and geography contexts.

Paddy (meaning 2) — A fit of anger or a childish tantrum. Informal British and Irish English only.

If someone in India, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, or Japan says "paddy," they almost certainly mean rice or rice fields. If someone in Britain or Ireland says "paddy," it could mean either — but outside of agricultural talk, it probably means a bad temper.
